title: Docker fundamentals
description: A practical reference to images, containers, Dockerfiles, volumes, networking, and Compose.

sections.title: Containers and Docker
sections.description:
A container packages an application and its user-space dependencies into an image, then runs it as an isolated process. Linux containers share the host Linux kernel; they are not virtual machines and do not each boot a guest operating system. Docker Desktop provides a Linux environment for Linux containers on macOS and Windows.

Containers can improve consistency but do not guarantee that software works on every machine. CPU architecture, kernel features, configuration, secrets, and external services still matter. Monoliths and microservices are architecture choices, not Docker features.

sections.title: Images, containers, and commands
sections.description:
An image is an immutable template made of layers; a container is a running or stopped instance of an image. Tags are convenient labels, but tags such as `latest` can move. Pin trusted production dependencies to reviewed versions or digests when reproducibility matters.

Publishing `8080:80` maps host port 8080 to container port 80. Bind to `127.0.0.1` when a service should only be reachable from the local machine.

codeExamples.code:
docker version
docker pull nginx:1.27
docker image ls
docker run --detach --name web --publish 8080:80 nginx:1.27
docker ps
docker logs web
docker stop web
docker rm web

sections.title: Dockerfiles and image builds
sections.description:
A Dockerfile describes how to assemble an image. Keep the build context small with `.dockerignore`; copy dependency manifests first when that enables build caching. Use a trusted, maintained base image and a non-root runtime user where possible.

Do not copy credentials into an image or build context. Use build secrets for build-time credentials and runtime secret facilities for application secrets. `EXPOSE` documents a port; it does not publish it.

codeExamples.code:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --chown=node:node . .
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

docker build --tag example-app:1.0 .
docker image inspect example-app:1.0

sections.title: Production-minded image practices
sections.description:
- Prefer small, maintained base images and rebuild regularly for security updates.
- Use multi-stage builds to keep compilers and development dependencies out of runtime images.
- Run as a non-root user and avoid unnecessary Linux capabilities.
- Pin and review dependencies; scan images, then triage findings in context.
- Set CPU and memory limits appropriate to the workload and monitor runtime behavior.
- Avoid embedding secrets in image layers, build arguments, or source control.

sections.title: Persistent storage
sections.description:
A container's writable layer is usually disposable. Use a named volume for persistent data managed by Docker, or a bind mount when a container must use a specific host path. Mount permissions and platform path behavior need attention.

Volumes persist beyond an individual container, but they still need backups, access controls, and a restore plan. Do not assume volume data is replicated or automatically backed up.

codeExamples.code:
docker volume create app-data
docker run --mount source=app-data,target=/var/lib/app example-app:1.0

sections.title: Container networking
sections.description:
Containers on a user-defined bridge network can resolve each other by container or service name. Inside a container, `localhost` refers to that same container, not another service or the host.

Publish only the ports that need host access. On shared or production hosts, use firewall rules and explicit network boundaries; a Docker network alone is not a complete security boundary.

codeExamples.code:
docker network create app-network
docker run --network app-network --name db example-database:1.0
docker run --network app-network --name app example-app:1.0

sections.title: Docker Compose
sections.description:
Compose describes related containers, networks, and volumes in a YAML file. Use it to make a repeatable local development environment; production deployment still needs a suitable operational platform and controls.

`depends_on` controls startup ordering, not application readiness. Use health checks and retry logic when one service must wait for another. Keep `.env` files with real secrets out of version control.

codeExamples.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - database-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  database-data:

docker compose up --build --detach
docker compose ps
docker compose logs --follow
docker compose down

sections.title: Registries and image scanning
sections.description:
A registry stores and distributes images. Authenticate using the registry's supported credential helper rather than placing passwords in shell history. Before deployment, verify image provenance and scan images with a maintained scanner such as [Trivy](https://trivy.dev/).

Never treat a clean scan as proof that an image is secure. Review the base image, dependencies, configuration, access permissions, and runtime behavior as well.

codeExamples.code:
docker login
docker tag example-app:1.0 registry.example.com/team/example-app:1.0
docker push registry.example.com/team/example-app:1.0

sections.title: Troubleshooting and safe cleanup
sections.description:
Inspect before deleting. `docker system prune` removes unused resources and can remove data you still need; `docker system prune --all --volumes` is especially destructive. Back up important volumes and verify the exact target before cleanup.

Further reading: [Docker documentation](https://docs.docker.com/) and [Docker Compose documentation](https://docs.docker.com/compose/).

codeExamples.code:
docker ps --all
docker logs --tail 100 web
docker inspect web
docker system df
docker compose config
